newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr fails to profit from rate calm.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr fails to profit from rate calm.

text.p: The Australian dollar eked out a meagre US$0.7635/7675 range for a fourth straight session Wednesday, and dealers suspected its inability to sustain a rally presaged a renewed downtrend.
Bulls were especially disappointed at the failure to capitalise on Tuesday's robust economic outlook from the Reserve Bank which extinguished all thoughts of a near term easing.

A firm set of capital imports data today further supported the bank's upbeat assessment on business investment, but again the currency could make no ground and instead faced Japanese selling and profit taking on the European crosses.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar was hard pressed at US$0.7637/42 having eased from US$0.7667/72 late here Tuesday.
Traders said support had so far proved solid at US$0.7635 while resistance at US$0.7675 had defeated repeated efforts to extend last week's bounce from US$0.7550.
The currency had begun to wilt offshore as a German bank took profits on its recent sharp gains over the mark -- rumours of the amount sold ranged right up to A$1.0 billion.
The inclination to book profit was encouraged by comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer that the U.S. dollar's rise on the mark wasover due, but he now hoped it had ended.
The currency extended an overnight fall in response to stand at 1.2872/84 marks from Tuesday's four-year high of 1.3055/66.
The U.S. dollar also corrected to 1.6860/65 marks from 1.7030/35, but dealers doubted the mark could sustain a recovery while Germany's economic fundamentals remained so dire.
Indeed, they noted Tietmeyer had also conceded that further rate cuts might be needed to revive the German economy, an outlook that was hardly supportive of a stronger currency.
In contrast the Australian economy was starting to show signs of a revival after slowing through much of 1996, which had convinced the RBA another easing was not warranted for now.

Oe such sign was merchandise imports for January which jumped 5.8 percent, before rounding, compared to forecasts of a 2.0 percent gain. The imports total was the second highest on record with all the gain in capital goods imports which leapt a whopping 28.7 percent.

The growth owed much to the import of several shipping vessels but analysts emphasised these were investment goods like any other and should not be discounted as "one-off" items as some commentators were apt to do. "It just shows companies must be confident to make such big investments," said Stephen Koukoulas chief econmist at Citibank Australia.
The latest data on business investment intentions showed they planned to up spending by around 17 percent in 1996/97, a figure which the RBA thought eminently reachable.

Dealers were not sure that steady rates alone would be enough to attract fresh demand from Japan since the big securities houses there were concentrating on spreading their currency risk at the moment.
Nevertheless, they noted talk of a rate hike in the U.K. had faded in recent days dulling the attraction of sterling as an alternative to A$ assets.
